title: The Right Side of the Bridge

where.detail: the near end of the mill bridge at dusk, under the mill's lamps

time: the afternoon of the weir into dusk
last_beat: At the far edge of the field across the river, shapes stood at the edge of the trees and began, slowly, to walk out; nobody said what they were, and Wren counted them, lost her place at forty, and started again at one.

people.did: Sat for Maelis's needle, took the stick back from Ash, saw the far-bank line drawn up the way the clan line stood at Harrow Ford, said why first, and asked for the bridge kept open all night, one cart at a time.
people.now: At the near end of the mill bridge at dusk on the stick, his arm sewn and bandaged, the carts crossing one at a time under lamps and shapes moving at the far edge of the field.

facts.fact: When a miller named him the captain of the Ninth off the post, he did not turn his head.
facts.evidence: Darrow did not turn his head. He had learned that once, young, at a rail

facts.fact: Seeing the far-bank line drawn up as the clan line had been at Harrow Ford, he told the company and the miller his reason first: he was on the wrong side of that line once and wants to be on the right side of one.
facts.evidence: I've seen a line stood like that once. I was on the wrong side of it

facts.fact: He asked for the mill bridge kept open through the night, one cart at a time under lamps.
facts.evidence: So: we keep this bridge open tonight.

people.did: Sewed his sword arm on the cart's tail and told him the two fingers are as they were.
people.now: At the bridge, counting how long he stands.

facts.fact: She sewed the cut on his sword arm and told him the arm will mend and the two slow fingers will not; nothing about the weir changed that.
facts.evidence: The arm will mend," she said. "Those won't.

people.did: Gave the bank his speech on a man who won a duel by standing on a rock, and was pleased that nobody sleeps.
people.now: At the bridge, freeing locked carts with a pole and a great deal of language.

facts.fact: He told the whole bank he had spent thirty years telling young knights to stand still, and was proud of the Captain for finally learning it.

people.did: Kept her eyes on the ledger, forgot to be cross when the dog fetched, took the count of the carts, and began counting the shapes at the field's edge.
people.now: At the bridge with the ledger, counting carts and the shapes across the field.

facts.fact: At dusk she counted the shapes at the edge of the trees across the river under her breath, lost her place at forty and started again.
facts.evidence: She lost her place at forty, and started again at one.

people.did: Read the far-bank line before he could and said it was people with something behind them; said aye to keeping the bridge open.
people.now: At the bridge, the carts coming over one at a time.

facts.fact: She read the far-bank line before Darrow said it: not a queue for a toll, but people with something behind them.
facts.evidence: That's people with something behind them.

people.did: Went down below the fall into the broken ice and brought Darrow's stick up in her teeth, once.
people.now: Across Darrow's boots at the near end of the bridge.

facts.fact: Ash, who does not fetch, brought Darrow's lost stick up out of the ice below the weir in her teeth.

codex.name: The mill bridge
codex.text: One span of old timber across the river above the river mill, wide enough for one cart, with the mill's toll-board nailed at the near end: no cart to cross after the dusk bell, ahead of the miller's, or that the bridge will not bear (Ch 7 epigraph; Sc 1).

fired.evidence: Darrow did not turn his head. He had learned that once, young, at a rail, and he had kept it.

struggle: The mill bridge: carts from the far bank crossing one at a time under the mill's lamps through the night, and at the edge of the field behind them, shapes that have begun to walk out of the trees.

add: the borrowed stick, used on the Steps and kept

now.against: Whatever stands at the edge of the trees across the river, behind the carts.
now.next: The night on the bridge, one cart at a time.

title: Name the Load

where.detail: the mill road at the end of the lamps, the crossed carts drawn up along it

time: dusk into night on the day of the weir
last_beat: At the end of the lamps Rae told him that had been a walk, in case he was wondering, and waited for him to come level before she walked back toward the bridge.

people.did: Asked Rae, badly, to walk up the line of crossed carts with him; named the loads with her and named the loom but missed the old woman riding under it.
people.now: Walking back toward the bridge lamps beside Rae on the stick.

facts.fact: On the night of the bridge he asked Rae to walk up the line of carts with him, without quite saying that was what he was asking.
facts.evidence: So you could come. If you wanted. Tell me what I'm looking at.

people.did: Heard what he was asking, said aye to the end of the lamps and back, made it a game of naming the loads, laughed out loud at his loom, and told him it had been a walk.
people.now: Walking back toward the bridge with the lamp, at his pace.

facts.fact: She told him he had asked her two things and said only one of them.
facts.evidence: That's two things you've asked me

facts.fact: She laughed out loud when he named a loom and missed the old woman riding under it, and said she would tell Wren for the book.
facts.evidence: I'm telling Wren, then. She'll want it for the book.

facts.fact: At the end of the lamps she told him it had been a walk, and that she would have said if it wasn't.
